column1: Why does applying a film finish to poorly prepared wood make defects MORE visible rather than hiding them?
column2: Film finishes (polyurethane, shellac, oil-varnish blends) increase the optical contrast between light and shadow at the surface, so scratches, mill marks, and torn fibers become magnified rather than concealed.

column1: What causes 'picture framing' (uneven gloss) when finishing ring-porous woods like white oak or ash without pore-filling?
column2: Large open earlywood vessels draw finish deep into their pores while dense, uniform latewood resists penetration, creating uneven absorption and gloss variation across the surface.

column1: Why is hard maple, despite being 'beginner-friendly' to work, actually difficult to finish cleanly?
column2: Maple is diffuse-porous with uniform absorption, so any surface scratch becomes a uniform channel for finish/stain absorption, turning scratches into highly visible dark lines.

column1: What is the fundamental mechanistic difference between pigments and dyes in wood coloring?
column2: Pigments are solid particles (0.1–10 μm) that lodge in surface topography and scatter light at particle boundaries (mechanical deposition, obscures grain). Dyes are molecules (1–2 nm) that dissolve into true solution and penetrate cell walls via diffusion, absorbing specific wavelengths without scattering (transparent, reveals grain).

column1: According to the Washburn equation, what governs penetration depth of a dye into wood, and how does solvent choice affect this?
column2: Penetration depth increases with the square root of time, scaled by surface tension, contact angle, and viscosity. Fast-evaporating alcohol carriers deposit dye quickly near the surface; slower water-based carriers allow deeper migration; oil-based carriers penetrate slowest but extend working time to hours.

column1: What are the three fundamental mechanisms by which liquid wood finishes become solid films?
column2: 1) Evaporative (solids deposit via solvent escape, e.g., shellac, nitrocellulose lacquer), 2) Reactive (molecular cross-linking via oxidation, moisture, or catalysis), 3) Coalescing (hybrid waterborne mechanism where latex particles lose water carrier then fuse via co-solvent).

column1: Why can shellac be amalgamated, padded out, or stripped with ethanol at any point in the future, even after full cure?
column2: Shellac is a thermoplastic evaporative finish—no chemical bonds form during cure, so the resin polymer remains permanently soluble in its original solvent (ethanol), allowing new coats to bond perfectly to old ones and full reversibility.

column1: What are the two distinct mechanisms by which UV radiation degrades a finished wood surface?
column2: 1) Direct photodegradation: UV photons (290-400nm) cleave C-C, C-O, and C-N bonds in the coating polymer backbone, causing chalking and loss of gloss/cohesion. 2) Substrate degradation: UV penetrates the film and photo-oxidizes lignin in the wood beneath, producing yellow-to-gray discoloration and weakening the wood-coating bond—even while the film still looks intact.

column1: How do UV absorbers (benzotriazole/benzophenone) differ from HALS (hindered amine light stabilizers) in protecting finishes?
column2: UV absorbers act as sacrificial targets that absorb UV energy and dissipate it as heat before it reaches the polymer or wood. HALS do not absorb UV directly; instead they are radical scavengers that interrupt the free-radical chain reactions propagating photodegradation. The most durable systems (e.g., marine spar varnish) combine both.

column1: What is the acceptable environmental working envelope for most film-building finishes, and what happens outside it?
column2: 65–80°F (18–27°C) and 40–60% RH. Below 60°F, oil-based finishes cross-link too slowly (feels dry but isn't fully polymerized, risking sand-through). Above 80°F with high humidity, waterborne finishes flash too fast, trapping solvent and producing a milky film.

column1: Why is wood moisture content (MC) critical to check before finishing, and what threshold signals a problem?
column2: Surface wood testing at 12% MC or above (in a shop at 40% RH) is storing water that will migrate out as the finish cures, disrupting adhesion and causing raised grain through the film.

column1: Why does quartersawn lumber behave differently from plain-sawn lumber when finishing?
column2: Quartersawn stock is cut closer to radially, exposing tighter, more uniform end-grain-adjacent structure that is more dimensionally stable under humidity cycles, compared to plain-sawn boards which expose wide tangential face grain with cathedral patterns and more uneven finish absorption.
